segments.title: Chương 305: 0307【Thẩm định trước niêm yết】
segments.content:
In May, the entire management of ByteDance got busy.

Not just with daily administration, but also with drafting the registration statement.

Including Chen Guiliang, all members of management had to be deeply involved, describing in detail in the registration statement the business model, market, competition, technology, operations, and so on, and explaining the financial performance and situation. The backgrounds of management and major shareholders, their salaries, their shareholdings, how the funds raised from the IPO were planned to be spent, etc.

They also had to disclose the various risks their company faced.

"The VIE risks aren't written clearly enough. Mr. Chen, please don't be too vague," the Chinese and American legal teams collectively told Chen Guiliang, holding the statement and asking for revisions.

Chen Guiliang was speechless.

He had already written about the risks associated with the VIE structure, yet the lawyers still considered it too vague.

Was he supposed to write in the registration statement: China issued Document No. 10 last year, which requires VIE structures to be reported and approved by the Chinese government, and the Ministry of Commerce will one hundred percent not approve it. Therefore, we did not report it and are operating in violation, hiding it from the Ministry of Commerce?

Lü Zhihui said, "It must all be written out clearly. That is: We control our Chinese operating entity through contractual arrangements, not direct equity ownership. If this arrangement is deemed invalid or unenforceable, it could lead to business termination or the value dropping to zero. Then, we must further elaborate on the core risk points in layers, including the fact that Chinese regulatory authorities have never formally recognized the legality of the VIE structure…"

It was basically like stripping naked for American reviewers to see.

Although the Ministry of Commerce issued Document No. 10 last year, one of its clauses explicitly targeted the VIE structure. But in practice, regulation was not strict. The official attitude was "no acknowledgment, no encouragement, no prohibition," maintaining a tacit, wait-and-see approach towards such listed companies.

Later on, regulations were strengthened because of an explosion abroad.

In 2011, Alibaba divested Alipay from its VIE structure, transferring it to a purely domestic company controlled by Jack Ma. The reason given was to obtain a third-party payment license issued by the central bank.

This could be interpreted as: Jack Ma unilaterally tore up the agreement with his investors!

This triggered a crisis of confidence in the VIE structure in the international capital market, causing the stock prices of Chinese concept stocks to plummet collectively at the time.

Only then did the relevant Chinese departments begin to strengthen regulations.

The policy was truly tightened during the pandemic, with factors of China-U.S. competition mixed in!

With the assistance of the person in charge of the IPO and the legal teams from both China and the US, Chen Guiliang and the senior management of ByteDance repeatedly revised the registration statement.

During this period, it was also sent to the investment bank and underwriter, Goldman Sachs, for their suggestions for further revision. Goldman Sachs's advice was particularly crucial, especially when it came to elaborating on the underwriting details.

This document went through repeated revisions for over half a month before it was finally ready to be submitted to the SEC for review.

The SEC would continuously raise inquiries, asking all sorts of questions, requiring Chen Guiliang to explain, clarify, or supplement.

If everything went smoothly, it would be over in a few weeks.

If there were complications, it could drag on for several months.

"Damn, the very first question they ask is so harsh!" Chen Guiliang was speechless when he saw the comment letter.

Chinese companies went public in the US every year, making this kind of question purely redundant: If China legislates to ban VIEs, will you admit your stock is worthless?

Chen Guiliang asked the lawyer, "How should I answer?"

The lawyer said, "Different companies have different ways of answering. If a company has state-owned shareholders, it can provide an endorsement letter from them. In any case, you answer in whatever way is most advantageous; it's impossible to give a direct answer. The official honors ByteDance has received, the policy support it has obtained, all of these can be sent over as documents."

Lü Zhihui said, "I've already had the lawyers prepare those documents. Including the 'Outstanding Chinese Cultural Website' plaque that Xiaonei has recently received for its active cooperation with the authorities. The level of the issuing authority for this plaque is very high, which will be very useful when answering the Americans' inquiries."

Chen Guiliang never would have thought that those "award certificates" issued by the government could actually be used to deal with the Americans.

Lü Zhihui added, "Also, I've prepared some case studies of VIE structure listings, along with the Chinese government's praise for those listed companies. The interrogators ask this kind of question to absolve themselves of responsibility. They're actually getting impatient asking it again and again."

This was not the only question; they raised a whole bunch.

It took a full five days for the lawyers to prepare all the response documents. Just as they were about to send them over, they suddenly discovered that the EDGAR system had crashed.

This thing was the official electronic database system of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.

In 2007, it crashed every other day.

So they resorted to the old method—fax!

"If things go smoothly, the SEC will send a second round of follow-up questions next week, in the form of a telephone inquiry and an EDGAR comment letter. I've already made a list of potential questions for the phone inquiry. If President Chen has any questions, consult the legal team."

Lü Zhihui said, "I need to fly to the US to discuss other matters with Goldman Sachs. In the later stages of the inquiry, we will also need to arrange rehearsals for the roadshow."

"Thank you for your hard work."

Another week passed.

The SEC's call was transferred through multiple layers, and Chen Guiliang and the lawyers had been waiting.

After the call connected, they had to confirm not only Chen Guiliang's identity but also the lawyer's. The content of every answer Chen Guiliang gave needed to be confirmed in writing by the lawyer.

The first question from the other side was one that wasn't on Lü Zhihui's list: "Your Xiaonei website uses a real-name system and, as required by the Chinese government, asks student users to provide their ID numbers. You have collected the ID numbers of tens of millions of students but did not disclose in the F-1 form whether this complies with the US Children's Online Privacy Protection Act. Are you aware that parental consent is required to provide services to users under the age of 13?"

Hearing this question, the lawyers from both China and the US looked at each other in dismay.

The Chinese lawyer was completely unaware of such a law in the United States.

The American lawyer, on the other hand, believed that since Xiaonei was in China, it didn't need to abide by American children's regulations, except for compliance in financial and other documents.

Therefore, in the registration statement that had been revised so many times, neither country's lawyers had disclosed this related issue.

Chen Guiliang could only handle it himself: "Xiaonei's users are primarily university students, with a portion of high school students. There are very few users under the age of 13. If discovered, we will require their guardians to provide a written letter of permission, or else we will suspend their accounts."

After this call, Chen Guiliang would have Xiaonei take action.

The questioner said, "You need to include this situation in your F-1 filing."

Chen Guiliang said, "This was our oversight. We will definitely make the revision."

The questioner then asked the fatal question for Web 2.0 companies: "Neither Xiaonei nor Hainei have mature profit models. Please explain how you will be profitable in the future."

Chen Guiliang said, "Our website's revenue has been continuously increasing. Especially the number of users paying for memberships and purchasing virtual items, which is growing steadily. Our SP business is also developing rapidly, with a sharp increase in revenue from ringback tones and microblogging... In addition, we are also developing a targeted advertising system. These are disclosed in the F-1 filing."

The questioner said, "Your two websites are very similar to Facebook. Facebook can't even do targeted advertising, and neither can portal websites like Yahoo. Why can you?"

This question was ridiculous; the relevant content had already been clearly stated in the registration statement.

It was clearly discriminatory against a Chinese company!

Chen Guiliang retorted, "If American websites can't do it, does that mean Chinese websites definitely can't? Many of my features and models are things Facebook doesn't have. If my company were in the US, Facebook would stand no chance against me. Also, e-commerce websites in both China and the US are already using this technology. And Xiaonei and Hainei will be the first and second SNS websites in the world to use this kind of technology!"

Chen Guiliang's spoken English was so-so; he would occasionally forget a word while speaking and have to ask the lawyer next to him.

The questioner said, "Mr. Chen, you don't need to get agitated. I am just conducting a reasonable inquiry. It's because there is no precedent for this kind of advertising model on similar websites in the United States. Now, please answer the third question…"
